question_bank.stem: Why did the lecture prefer the phrase agentic workflow over the single word agent?

options.text: Because workflow means the model is always trained with reinforcement learning, whereas agent means no learning is involved.
Because different teams use agent for everything from one prompt to a complex tool-using system, so workflow is more precise.
Because workflow refers only to deterministic software and agent refers only to language models with no external tools.
Because workflow guarantees multiple models, whereas agent always means a single model call.

question_bank.rationale: The lecture says agent is overloaded in industry, while agentic workflow better emphasizes the multi-step process.

source_ref.evidence_span: calling everything an agent doesn't do it justice.

frame_evidence.visual_description: Slide titled Definition quotes Andrew Ng and contrasts a simple RAG reply with a multi-step refund workflow.

question_bank.stem: Which description matches the lecture's definition of an agentic AI workflow?

options.text: A single prompt that always reasons internally without calling any tools or external systems.
A reinforcement-learning agent that must interact with an environment and optimize a reward signal.
A multi-step process that combines prompts, tools, and workflow logic to complete a task.
A pretraining pipeline that updates model weights continuously while users interact with it.

question_bank.rationale: The lecture defines an agentic workflow as a process built from prompts, tools, resources, and workflow logic.

source_ref.evidence_span: it's a bunch of prompts with tools,

frame_evidence.visual_description: Definition slide shows a refund-policy example and emphasizes that the workflow is the multi-step unit of interest.

question_bank.stem: A chatbot answers "Refunds are available within 30 days" but the user actually needs order-specific eligibility. What upgrade from the lecture best addresses that gap?

options.text: Use a shorter prompt that hides the policy text so the model is forced to guess based on general refund conventions.
Use a deterministic regex only, because any refund request can be fully resolved without asking the user for more information.
Use a few-shot prompt only, because examples remove the need for APIs or order-specific checks.
Use an agentic workflow that retrieves policy, asks for missing order information, queries the order system, and then confirms eligibility.

question_bank.rationale: The refund example in the lecture moves from one-step policy answering to a multi-step workflow with retrieval, clarification, and API use.

source_ref.evidence_span: So it's all about the multi-step process to complete a task.

frame_evidence.visual_description: Refund-policy slide visually contrasts a one-shot RAG answer with an AI-agent path that asks for an order number and checks an API.

question_bank.stem: The lecture describes a shift from deterministic software to fuzzy engineering. What changes in that shift?

options.text: Systems increasingly interpret free-form text, images, and ambiguous user intent instead of only processing rigid structured inputs.
Systems increasingly replace all APIs with vector databases so every workflow becomes retrieval-only.
Systems increasingly avoid user interaction so outputs can be scored entirely by deterministic unit tests.
Systems increasingly require no guardrails because generative models already internalize enterprise policy perfectly.

question_bank.rationale: The lecture frames agentic AI as moving software toward fuzzier interpretation of unstructured inputs and open-ended intent.

frame_evidence.visual_description: Lecture slides transition from definitions to examples of workflows that must reason over less-structured user requests.

question_bank.stem: Why did the lecture argue for guardrails and sometimes human review in fuzzy AI workflows?

options.text: Because fuzzy workflows cannot call tools, so humans must always perform every external action on the model's behalf.
Because generated scores or decisions can be wrong, so human-in-the-loop checks help catch failures that deterministic pipelines would not naturally expose.
Because fuzzy workflows always maximize latency, so human review is mainly a way to slow the system down even more.
Because fuzzy workflows eliminate the need for evaluation, so humans are used only to provide cosmetic explanations afterward.

question_bank.rationale: The lecture emphasizes guardrails and human review when fuzzy tasks such as assessments or content generation can still fail.

source_ref.evidence_span: And how am I going to design those guardrails?

frame_evidence.visual_description: Lecture remains on enterprise-workflow examples while the instructor explains why ambiguous model behavior calls for guardrails and review.
